title: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE
summary: Load the roastery tables with INSERT, read rows back with SELECT, change them with UPDATE and remove them with DELETE, and use MySQL's LAST_INSERT_ID() and INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
introduction: Create, read, update and delete are the four operations every application performs, and in SQL they are INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. This lesson fills the three roastery tables with the sample data that the rest of the tutorial uses, then changes and removes rows the safe way. Along the way you learn to read the Query OK lines the mysql client prints, fetch the id MySQL just generated, and write an upsert the MySQL way.
learningObjectives: Insert single and multiple rows and read back generated ids with LAST_INSERT_ID()
Read the Query OK, Rows matched and Changed counters the client prints
Update and delete rows safely with a WHERE clause
Write an upsert with INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE

blocks.text: List the columns explicitly, then one tuple per row. Columns you leave out receive their default: `id` is generated by `AUTO_INCREMENT`, and `joined_on` has no default, so it must be supplied. A multi-row `INSERT` is far faster than one statement per row because the server parses once and writes once. The `Records` line confirms the count; `Duplicates` and `Warnings` should be zero.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, joined_on) VALUES
  ('Priya Nair',    'priya@example.com',  'Bengaluru', '2025-01-12'),
  ('Tomás Ribeiro', 'tomas@example.com',  'Lisbon',    '2025-02-03'),
  ('Mei Chen',      'mei@example.com',    'Taipei',    '2025-02-28'),
  ('Yusuf Demir',   'yusuf@example.com',  'Istanbul',  '2025-03-19'),
  ('Hannah Weiss',  'hannah@example.com', 'Berlin',    '2025-04-07');

blocks.content:
Query OK, 5 rows affected (0.01 sec)
Records: 5  Duplicates: 0  Warnings: 0

blocks.text: The coffees and orders follow the same pattern. Dates and times are quoted strings in ISO order; `NULL` is written without quotes, and here it records that most orders have not shipped yet.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO coffees (name, origin, roast, price, stock) VALUES
  ('Morning Blend',      'Brazil',    'medium', 12.50, 40),
  ('Yirgacheffe',        'Ethiopia',  'light',  16.00, 25),
  ('Sumatra Mandheling', 'Indonesia', 'dark',   15.25,  0),
  ('Decaf Colombia',     'Colombia',  'medium', 13.75, 10),
  ('Espresso Roast',     'Brazil',    'dark',   14.00, 60);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, coffee_id, quantity, status, ordered_at, shipped_at) VALUES
  (1, 1, 2, 'shipped',   '2025-05-02 09:15:00', '2025-05-03 10:00:00'),
  (1, 2, 1, 'shipped',   '2025-05-02 09:15:00', '2025-05-03 10:00:00'),
  (2, 5, 3, 'paid',      '2025-05-10 14:02:00', NULL),
  (3, 2, 2, 'pending',   '2025-05-11 18:30:00', NULL),
  (4, 1, 1, 'cancelled', '2025-05-15 08:45:00', NULL),

blocks.text: Had an order named a customer id that does not exist, the foreign key would have rejected the whole statement with error 1452 (*a foreign key constraint fails*). That is the constraint doing its job: no row is written unless every row is valid.

`SELECT *` returns every column in definition order. It is fine in the client; in application code, name the columns you need so that adding a column later cannot break anything. The next lesson covers filtering and sorting in depth; here a simple `WHERE` is enough to find the coffee that is sold out.

blocks.code: SELECT id, name, price, stock FROM coffees WHERE stock = 0;

blocks.text: `UPDATE` changes the columns in `SET` for every row that matches `WHERE`. The client prints two numbers that beginners confuse: `Rows matched` is how many rows the `WHERE` selected, `Changed` is how many actually had a different value afterwards. Run the same statement twice and the second run reports `Changed: 0`, which is correct, not a failure.

blocks.code:
UPDATE coffees SET stock = 30 WHERE id = 3;

SELECT id, name, stock FROM coffees WHERE id = 3;

blocks.title: An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE touches every row
blocks.text: `UPDATE coffees SET stock = 30;` silently restocks the whole catalogue and `DELETE FROM orders;` empties the table; the client just prints `Query OK, 5 rows affected`. Run the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` first to see which rows it picks, and for anything that matters wrap the change in a transaction so you can `ROLLBACK` (see [Transactions](/tutorials/mysql/transactions)). MySQL Workbench and `mysql --safe-updates` refuse such statements with error 1175 unless the WHERE uses a key column.
Upsert: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE

An *upsert* inserts a row, or updates the existing one when a primary key or unique index already holds that value. MySQL spells it `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`; PostgreSQL and SQLite use `ON CONFLICT`. The row alias `AS new` (available since 8.0.20) lets the update part refer to the values you tried to insert and replaces the deprecated `VALUES()` function. The affected-rows count tells you what happened: 1 for an insert, 2 for an update, 0 if the row already matched.

Row 4 existed, so instead of a duplicate-key error the stock went from 10 to 18. The related `REPLACE INTO` statement deletes the old row and inserts the new one, which fires `ON DELETE` actions on foreign keys and resets columns you did not mention; prefer the upsert.

After an insert, `LAST_INSERT_ID()` returns the `AUTO_INCREMENT` value generated for *your* connection, unaffected by other clients. Database drivers expose the same number (`insertId` in Node's mysql2, `lastrowid` in Python's connectors). MySQL has no `RETURNING` clause, unlike PostgreSQL, SQLite and MariaDB.

blocks.content:
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.01 sec)

+------------------+
| LAST_INSERT_ID() |
+------------------+
|                6 |
+------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

Query OK, 1 row affected (0.01 sec)

blocks.text: The deleted id is not reused: the next customer will be 7. Deleting a customer who has orders fails with `ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails`, naming `fk_orders_customer`. If orders should disappear with their customer, declare the key with `ON DELETE CASCADE`; if they must be kept, delete or reassign them first. `TRUNCATE TABLE` empties a table and resets `AUTO_INCREMENT` to 1, but it cannot be rolled back and refuses tables that other tables reference.

blocks.title: The data from here on
blocks.text: After this lesson the tables hold exactly the rows above, with Sumatra Mandheling at 30 in stock and Decaf Colombia at 18, five customers and seven orders. Every output in the following lessons assumes that state.

questions.question: An UPDATE prints `Rows matched: 3  Changed: 0`. What happened?
questions.explanation: Three rows satisfied the WHERE clause, but each already held the value being set, so nothing was written. This is normal, not an error.
options: Three rows matched but already had the new values
The statement failed on three rows

questions.question: In MySQL 8.4 you can write `INSERT INTO customers (...) VALUES (...) RETURNING id;` to get the generated id.
questions.explanation: MySQL has no RETURNING clause. Run the INSERT and then call `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, or read the id from your driver.
